chapters.title: Chapter 3: Beyond VaR: Coherent Risk Measures and Backtesting

lessons.title: Backtesting VaR Models: Kupiec Test and Exception Analysis

children.text: Every method in this course, Historical Simulation, Parametric, Monte Carlo, produces a number that comes with a promise. A 99% 1-day VaR promises that actual losses should exceed it on roughly 1% of trading days, no more, no less. Backtesting is the discipline of holding that promise to account: recording every day the model was actually breached, and checking whether the breach rate matches what the model claimed. A VaR model nobody backtests is a VaR model nobody has actually verified.

body.label: Exception
body.value: A trading day where the actual realized loss exceeds the VaR figure predicted for that day
body.context: Also called a breach. Counting exceptions over time is the foundation of every backtesting method.

children.text: Counting Exceptions: The First, Simplest Check

body.caption: Alpha is the confidence level, N is the number of trading days backtested. A 99% VaR model tested over a year of trading should show close to this many breaches, not zero.

children.text: A desk backtests its 99% 1-day VaR model over the last 250 NSE trading days, roughly one calendar year. At 99% confidence, the model should be breached about (1 - 0.99) x 250, or 2.5 times, over that period. The actual count that year was 6.

stats.label: Observed exceptions
stats.context: Actual breaches over the same 250-day period

stats.label: Ratio
stats.context: More breaches than the model promised

children.text: Before any statistical test, regulators use a simpler tool: a traffic light. For a 99% 1-day VaR model backtested over 250 trading days, the Basel Committee's supervisory framework sorts the exception count into three zones.

body.caption: Basel traffic light zones for 99% VaR backtesting over 250 trading days

cells: Consistent with a correctly calibrated model, no action needed
Cause for concern, regulators increase the capital multiplier applied to the model and expect an explanation
Strong evidence the model understates risk, triggers mandatory review and a maximum capital multiplier

body.text: 6 exceptions out of 250 days lands the desk in the Yellow zone. This alone does not prove the model is broken, a well-calibrated model will occasionally show more exceptions than expected purely by chance, but it is enough to trigger a capital penalty and a formal explanation to the risk committee or regulator. This is where a proper statistical test earns its place: is 6 exceptions genuinely surprising, or is it within the range normal statistical noise would produce?

children.text: The Kupiec Test: Is 6 Exceptions Too Many?

The Kupiec test, also called the Proportion of Failures test, formalizes exactly this question with a likelihood-ratio hypothesis test. The null hypothesis is that the model is correctly calibrated, that the true exception probability equals the model's stated (1 minus confidence). The test statistic follows a chi-square distribution with 1 degree of freedom, and at a 95% significance level, the critical value is 3.841. If the computed statistic exceeds 3.841, you reject the null hypothesis, the model's exception rate is statistically too far from what it promised.

body.caption: The Kupiec Proportion of Failures statistic. p is the model's stated exception probability (1 minus confidence), N is the number of days tested, x is the observed exception count.

stats.label: Chi-square critical value (95% significance, 1 df)
stats.context: The threshold for rejecting the model

stats.label: Conclusion
stats.context: 3.555 is below 3.841, not statistically significant at the 95% level

body.text: Notice the two frameworks give slightly different signals here. Basel's traffic light already flags 6 exceptions as Yellow, triggering a capital penalty. The Kupiec test, run at 95% significance, says 6 exceptions is not yet statistically distinguishable from bad luck under a correctly calibrated model. Both are legitimate tools asking different questions, Basel's zones are a practical, precautionary trigger, Kupiec is a formal statistical judgment. Recomputing the same test across the Yellow zone shows the Kupiec statistic actually crosses 3.841 and starts rejecting the model at 7 exceptions, not 5, so the two frameworks mostly, but not perfectly, agree on where real concern begins.

The Kupiec test has a real limitation worth knowing: it only checks how many exceptions occurred, not when. A model with 6 exceptions spread evenly across the year looks statistically identical to the Kupiec test as one with all 6 exceptions clustered in the same stressed week, even though the second pattern is a far more dangerous sign about how the model behaves specifically during a crisis. Tests that account for this clustering, such as Christoffersen's conditional coverage test, exist precisely to catch what Kupiec misses, and are beyond this course's scope, but worth knowing by name if you go further into model validation.

body.title: Expected Exceptions at a Different Confidence Level
body.prompt: A desk backtests its 95% 1-day VaR model over 250 trading days. How many exceptions should it expect, on average?
body.explanation: Expected exceptions = (1 - 0.95) x 250 = 0.05 x 250 = 12.5. A 95% VaR model is supposed to be breached far more often than a 99% model, roughly once every 20 days rather than once every 100.

body.title: Interpreting a Red Zone Result
body.scenario: A different desk's 99% VaR model shows 11 exceptions over the same 250-day period, landing it in Basel's Red zone. The desk head argues this is likely just a statistical fluke, since 6 exceptions elsewhere in the firm was already judged statistically insignificant by the Kupiec test.
body.prompt: Is the desk head's argument reasonable? What would you check before accepting or rejecting it?
body.modelAnswer: The argument does not hold up. Applying the same Kupiec test logic used at 6 exceptions, the statistic at 11 exceptions out of 250 is far larger and clearly exceeds the 3.841 critical value, this is a statistically significant departure from the model's promised 99% coverage, not a borderline case like 6. Before accepting any explanation, check whether the exceptions are clustered in time, which would point to a specific regime the model handles poorly, review whether the volatility or correlation inputs feeding the model have gone stale, and check whether the position or portfolio composition changed materially during the backtest window in a way the model was not recalibrated for.

body.text: A VaR model is a promise about the future, backed by nothing until you check the past. Backtesting is how that promise gets checked, and both a practical traffic light and a formal statistical test are needed to know when to actually worry.

points: Backtesting compares a VaR model's promised exception rate, (1 minus confidence) times the number of trading days, against its actual observed exception count.
Basel's traffic light framework sorts 99% VaR backtests over 250 days into Green (0 to 4 exceptions), Yellow (5 to 9), and Red (10 or more) zones, with rising capital penalties.
The Kupiec Proportion of Failures test formalizes the same question statistically, comparing a likelihood-ratio statistic against a chi-square critical value of 3.841 at 95% significance.

The two frameworks can disagree at the margins, Basel flagged 6 exceptions as Yellow while Kupiec only starts rejecting the model at 7 exceptions in this course's worked example, which is why serious model validation uses more than one check.

Kupiec only tests exception frequency, not timing, so a model can pass it while still failing badly during a specific stressed period, exactly the gap that stress testing, starting in the next chapter, is built to address.
